title: The wall that heals itself
style: documentary photograph, weathered marine masonry, overcast Mediterranean light, muted colour, fine grain, no text, no watermark, no modern objects
negative: text, letters, words, watermark, logo, cartoon, cgi, painting, illustration, modern construction, people

lines.vo: A Roman harbour wall poured into the sea in 40 BC still stands in the surf.
lines.image: a weathered concrete mole running into grey-green water

lines.vo: Modern marine concrete cracks and fails in fifty years. Often in thirty.
lines.image: spalled modern concrete with rusted reinforcement showing

lines.vo: The Romans mixed volcanic ash from Pozzuoli with lime, and poured it in seawater.
lines.image: coarse grey volcanic ash in a heap

lines.vo: Seawater is what destroys modern concrete. Here it was an ingredient.
lines.image: green seawater breaking over dark stone

lines.vo: The mix left lumps of unslaked lime through the wall. We read those as sloppy work.
lines.image: a broken concrete face showing white inclusions

lines.vo: When a crack opens, water runs down it and reaches one of the lumps.
lines.image: a hairline crack across weathered grey concrete

lines.vo: The lime dissolves, recrystallises across the gap, and seals it shut.
lines.image: white mineral crystals grown across a dark fracture

lines.vo: Two thousand years of storms have made that harbour stronger, not weaker.
lines.image: a storm sea against an old breakwater

lines.vo: We only worked out why in 2017. The recipe was written down in the first century.
lines.image: an old page of latin text under glass
lines.title: TWO THOUSAND
